hops.title: A pain pathway hiding in the touch column
hops.text: Many classic accounts described the dorsal column as carrying touch and body position, with pain thought to travel elsewhere. Then, in 1996 and 1997, a Texas team that included Hirshberg, Nauta and Willis reported something odd. In a handful of patients with severe pelvic pain, most of it from cancer, surgeons made a small cut or puncture near the middle of the dorsal column. The pain eased, yet a pinprick on the skin still felt sharp. Rat experiments suggested why: PSDC neurons in the lower spinal cord respond to painful stimulation of pelvic organs and send their axons up near that midline.

sources.citation: Hirshberg RM, Al-Chaer ED, Lawand NB, Westlund KN, Willis WD. Is there a pathway in the posterior funiculus that signals visceral pain? Pain. 1996;67(2-3):291-305.
Nauta HJ, Hewitt E, Westlund KN, Willis WD Jr. Surgical interruption of a midline dorsal column visceral pain pathway. Case report and review of the literature. J Neurosurg. 1997;86(3):538-542.

image.caption: In rats, PSDC axons near the dorsal column's midline carry pelvic organ pain signals, not just touch.

hops.afterHeading: The key experiment: silence one route at a time
hops.title: Why a still finger misses fine texture
hops.text: Rest a fingertip still on fine sandpaper or fine fabric, then slide it slowly across. Notice whether the grain gets easier to read. In a 2000 study, people easily told fine abrasives apart as the surface slid across the skin, but did little better than guessing when it was held still; for coarse ones, accuracy stayed about the same either way. Without movement, roughness ratings for particles smaller than about 100 micrometers barely changed with size. Sliding turns tiny bumps into rapid skin vibrations. In a 2013 Stockholm study, blindfolded volunteers told a smooth surface from one with repeating wrinkles only 13 nanometers in amplitude and 760 nanometers apart.

sources.citation: Hollins M, Risner SR. Evidence for the duplex theory of tactile texture perception. Percept Psychophys. 2000;62(4):695-705.
Skedung L, Arvidsson M, Chung JY, Stafford CM, Berglund B, Rutland MW. Feeling small: exploring the tactile perception limits. Sci Rep. 2013;3:2617.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A hand sliding an index fingertip across fine sandpaper on a wooden table beside folded fabric and a mug.
image.caption: Sliding a fingertip turns tiny bumps into vibrations, revealing texture a still finger misses.

hops.title: Light touch and pain do not stay in separate lanes
hops.text: It is easy to assume a gentle brush could never hurt, because touch and pain run in sealed lanes. Nerve injuries say otherwise. In 1988, researchers studied seventeen patients whom light touch hurt. An ischemic block, which briefly cuts off a limb's blood supply, numbed touch while warm and cool sensing stayed intact, and abolished the touch-evoked pain in fifteen, pointing to myelinated fibers. A year later, blocking spinal glycine or GABA receptors in rats made light oscillating touch trigger an organized agitation response. Rat spinal cord slices later showed that blocking both together opened a multi-synapse path from mostly Aβ fibers onto lamina I neurons involved in pain signaling.

sources.citation: Campbell JN, Raja SN, Meyer RA, Mackinnon SE. Myelinated afferents signal the hyperalgesia associated with nerve injury. Pain. 1988;32(1):89-94.

Yaksh TL. Behavioral and autonomic correlates of the tactile evoked allodynia produced by spinal glycine inhibition: effects of modulatory receptor systems and excitatory amino acid antagonists. Pain. 1989;37(1):111-123.
Torsney C, MacDermott AB. Disinhibition opens the gate to pathological pain signaling in superficial neurokinin 1 receptor-expressing neurons in rat spinal cord. J Neurosci. 2006;26(6):1833-1843.

image.caption: When spinal glycine and GABA brakes fail, gentle touch can find a path into pain circuits.
